Kenji López-Alt Aug 5, 2026 View in app View in app A modernized tempura batter with vodka and club soda delivers restaurant-quality crispness without years of apprenticeship. What makes tempura—Japanese-style battered and fried vegetables and seafood—so unique? The key lies in the texture of the coating. Unlike more heavily-battered foods that can sometimes end up equal parts batter to food, with tempura, the coating should be lacy and whisper-thin, with plenty of bubbly nooks and crannies for adding texture and absorbing sauce. More than any other type of battering, tempura allows the flavor of the ingredients being battered to shine through. Tempura arrived in Japan with Portuguese missionaries in the sixteenth century. The Japanese word tempura comes the Portuguese word tempora , which referred to the days in which they abstained from meat, instead cooking battered-and-fried fish. Over the centuries Japanese cooks transformed it into something entirely its own, using lighter flours and specialized technique.
